decisions.quote: Despite the use of automated timing methods and a larger sample, our first experiment failed to show priming. Our second experiment was aimed at manipulating the beliefs of the experimenters: Half were led to think that participants would walk slower when primed congruently, and the other half was led to expect the opposite. Strikingly, we obtained a walking speed effect, but only when experimenters believed participants would indeed walk slower.
decisions.reason: The paper reports two replication experiments with conflicting results: Experiment 1 failed to replicate Bargh et al.'s walking-speed effect, whereas Experiment 2 replicated the effect (including on objective infrared timings) when experimenters expected slower walking. Because the authors conclude that priming and experimenter expectations jointly produce the effect rather than treating the replication as a pure methodological artifact, the aggregated outcome across the two experiments is mixed.

parent_objection: The first reply calls this mixed because Experiment1 fails and Experiment2 recovers walking-speed priming with induced experimenter expectations. The paper main Discussion says whether automatic behavioral priming can occur without awareness remains unclear; those showing slowing were often aware of it, and the authors call the measurement methods an object of research before established use. Resolve whether the central conclusion is a methodological/construct-validity critique (statistically successful but flawed), or qualified context-dependent replication legitimately mixed. Inspect abstract AND full Discussion and follow codebook main-message rule; do not merely count experiment outcomes or treat generic objective slowing as proving the original unconscious mechanism.

shipped.title_o: Automaticity of social behavior: Direct effects of trait construct and stereotype activation on action.
shipped.outcome_quote: First, in Experiment 1, despite the use of a larger sample and an experimental procedure devoid of the limitations present in the original experiment, we were not able to replicate Bargh et al’s [1] automatic effect of priming on walking speed.

blind_target.outcome_quote: Despite the use of automated timing methods and a larger sample, our first experiment failed to show priming. Our second experiment was aimed at manipulating the beliefs of the experimenters: Half were led to think that participants would walk slower when primed congruently, and the other half was led to expect the opposite. blind_target.outcome_reasoning: Authors explicitly report failure in Experiment 1 and conditional replication in Experiment 2, including objective timings. The paper questions automaticity, awareness and expectancy but does not give an overall verdict that overrides its opposing study results; aggregate mixed rather than treating one condition as the whole attempt.

original_review_items.parent_scope_question: Parent unresolved scope question: does experimenter-expectancy critique constitute the main methodological invalidity message, requiring statistically successful but flawed, or do authors present ordinary mixed replication? Apply special verdict and overall priority rules using authors own account.
